chunks: Sa'd narrated from Abu Ja'far, from 'Abad ibn Sulayman, from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari, who said:
A man wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'Does the fasting person smell the basil to enjoy its scent?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no harm in it.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (permissible)
key_terms.يَتَلَذَّذُ بِهِ: To enjoy/delight in it (referring to the scent)

ai.seo_question: Does smelling basil or other fragrant plants invalidate the fast in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Recorded in Shaykh al-Tusi’s *al-Istibsar*, this hadith from Imam al-Baqir (AS) clarifies that the act of smelling fragrant plants like basil for pleasure does not nullify the fast, distinguishing it from ingestion. This ruling is significant in Shia jurisprudence as it establishes that sensory enjoyment through the nose, without swallowing, remains compatible with the state of *ihram* in fasting. It reflects the broader principle that minor sensory pleasures do not detract from the spiritual discipline of *sawm*.
